sections.html:
An Arkansas homeowner can take up to $675 a year off the property tax bill on a qualifying home. House Bill 1103 of 2026 raised the figure from $600. Because older numbers still circulate, call your county assessor to confirm the amount before you quote it to a buyer or a tax preparer.

People say exemption, but what Arkansas provides is a credit. Amendment 79, section 3, directs the General Assembly to give an annual state credit against property tax on a homestead, and the credit can never exceed the tax owed. Picture a $650 bill: the credit wipes out $650 and the state does not mail you the difference.

sections.h2: Who qualifies and where to apply
sections.html:
The house must be your principal place of residence, and you must hold a qualifying ownership interest. File with the assessor's office in the county where the house sits.

  • Record owners qualify, as do buyers under a recorded sales contract and people holding a recorded life estate.
  • A home held in a revocable or irrevocable trust can qualify.
  • Someone who deeded the home away but kept a recorded life estate and still lives there can qualify.
  • A nursing home or retirement center resident who still owns the residence may qualify in some circumstances.
  • An LLC can qualify with a certificate of good standing and an attestation, signed by a member, that the house is that member's primary residence and no other credit is claimed.

Each owner gets one homestead credit per year. A rental, a vacant inherited house and a second home all fail the principal residence test.

Amendment 79 created three more tools alongside the credit: a freeze for owners 65 and older or disabled, a 5% yearly cap on homestead increases, and a 10% cap on other real property. Here is how the four compare.

ReliefWho gets itEffect on the taxHow to claim
Homestead creditOwner-occupantsUp to $675 off the yearly billApply with the county assessor
Age 65 or disabled freezeHomestead owners who qualify for the creditFreezes the taxable assessed valueApply with the county assessor
Homestead capHomesteads after a reappraisalTaxable value climbs 5% a year until it reaches full assessed valueBuilt into the assessment
Cap on other real propertyCommercial, agricultural and vacant parcelsTaxable value climbs 10% a year until full valueBuilt into the assessment

New construction, newly discovered property and substantial improvements fall outside the caps. A substantial improvement is renovation, reconstruction or refurbishment that adds 25% or more to the property's value.

Start at the assessor's office for the county where the house sits. Confirm that you live there as your principal residence and tell the clerk how you hold title: as record owner, under a recorded sales contract, as a life tenant, through a trust or through an LLC. Trust and LLC owners should expect to hand over extra paperwork, such as the good standing certificate and member attestation described above.

If you are 65 or older or disabled, ask about the freeze in the same visit and bring the proof listed in the next section. Ask what the filing window is for your county, and keep a copy of whatever you submit. A buyer or title company may later ask for it when the property is sold or refinanced.

sections.h2: How the age 65 or disabled freeze works
sections.html:
The freeze locks the home's taxable assessed value at the next assessment date after you turn 65 or become disabled. The tax bill itself is not locked. If a city, county or school district raises its millage, you still pay more.

Someone who is already 65 or disabled when they buy can have the value frozen at the next assessment date after the purchase. You must apply. Bring proof: a driver's license, state ID or birth certificate for age, or a Medicare card or Social Security award letter for disability.

Adding onto the house can end the freeze. The assessor removes it after an addition and you reapply at the new value.

sections.h2: What happens to the credit and the freeze when you sell?
sections.html:
Neither one goes with the house. A freeze cannot pass to the next owner of the same home, and a buyer cannot step into the seller's earlier limit.

Ark. Code § 26-26-1123 controls. After a sale, the assessor values the property at 20% of its appraised value on the next assessment date following the transfer of title. The new owner cannot claim an assessment limit until the second assessment date after the transfer. That is why a buyer's first bill can look much higher than yours did.

As the seller, do these three things:

  • Tell the assessor when the house stops being your principal residence.
  • Do not count on a second credit. If you buy another home, the one-credit-per-year rule still applies.
  • Decide in the contract who pays the bill that arrives after closing. Arkansas bills a year behind, so the 2026 assessment is billed in spring 2027 and due October 15, 2027.

sections.h2: Homestead tax credit versus creditor protection
sections.html:
The tax credit trims a property tax bill. Shielding a homestead from judgment creditors is a different subject, handled under Article 9 of the Arkansas Constitution.

Article 9, section 3 protects the homestead of a resident who is married or the head of a family from a judgment lien and from sale under execution, with exceptions the constitution lists. How that plays out for a given house, including in bankruptcy, needs a lawyer's reading. Filing for the tax credit neither creates nor removes that protection.

The credit ends with your ownership, and a cash price does not change that. What matters at sale time is the paperwork and any unpaid balance.

Property taxes are due to the county collector by October 15 each year. Unpaid balances after that date draw a 10% penalty, and real estate taxes also pick up 10% annual interest. Parcels that stay delinquent are certified to the Commissioner of State Lands, and title vests in the state. If you are behind, pay the balance before you list or sign a contract.

Expect these steps at a typical closing:

  • Ask the collector for a payoff figure by parcel number.
  • Have the title company pay any balance out of your proceeds.
  • Buy the transfer stamp for the deed.
  • Send the assessor a note that the property changed hands.

The deed carries its own tax. The real property transfer tax is $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration on transactions above $100, paid with a stamp on the deed. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and repair demands, but it does not skip these tax items.

faqs.q: Does Arkansas have a homestead exemption?
faqs.a: Arkansas gives a homestead property tax credit, not an exemption of value. It is worth up to $675 a year on a principal residence, and owners 65 or older or disabled can also apply to freeze the taxable assessed value.

faqs.q: Where do I apply for the Arkansas homestead credit?
faqs.a: Apply at the assessor's office in the county where the home sits. That office also handles the age 65 and disability freeze, so ask it for the form and the filing window.

faqs.q: Does the buyer inherit my homestead credit when I sell?
faqs.a: No. The buyer applies as a new owner. Under Ark. Code § 26-26-1123 the buyer gets no assessment limit until the second assessment date after the transfer, and a freeze cannot pass on.

faqs.q: Can I claim the credit on a rental or second home?
faqs.a: No. Only a homestead used as the owner's principal residence qualifies, and each owner can claim one credit per year.

faqs.q: Will turning 65 stop my property taxes from rising?
faqs.a: No. The freeze holds the taxable assessed value, not the bill. If a city, county or school district raises millage, your taxes can still go up.
